claims.text: Combined thermal aging and cyclic stress induce localized solute segregation at grain boundaries in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The induced grain-boundary segregation leads to short-range ordering.
Grain-boundary short-range order reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion caused by short-range order promotes brittle behavior.
Thermal activation enhances the mobility of specific alloying elements.
Repetitive mechanical stress enhances the mobility of specific alloying elements.
The enhanced elemental mobility causes selected elements to segregate to grain boundaries.
The proposed embrittlement can occur despite the alloy retaining an overall single-phase nature.
Relative to untreated specimens, thermally aged and cyclically loaded HEA specimens will contain detectable nanoscale segregated zones along grain boundaries.
The nanoscale grain-boundary segregated zones will exhibit short-range order.
Thermally aged and cyclically loaded HEA specimens will have lower impact toughness than untreated baseline specimens.
Brittleness in conventional alloys is predominantly associated with intergranular precipitation rather than stress-driven local ordering.
Embrittlement requires the simultaneous presence of elevated temperature and cyclic mechanical stress.
Below the thermal activation threshold, grain-boundary segregation and embrittlement will be minimal or absent.
Under static loading, grain-boundary segregation and embrittlement will be minimal or absent.
The untreated baseline HEA has a homogeneous solute distribution.
The untreated baseline HEA has satisfactory toughness.
